newsitem.title: UK: John Junor, legend of Fleet Street, dies at 78.
newsitem.headline: John Junor, legend of Fleet Street, dies at 78.

text.p: British editor and acerbic newspaper columnist Sir John Junor, one of the last giants of Fleet Street, died on Saturday, his newspaper said. He was 78.
Sir John was editor of the Sunday Express for 32 years, from the era of proprietor Lord Beaverbrook until 1986.
He was a legend in the newspaper industry for his acid humour as a columnist and his dogged rein at the Sunday Express.
His columns, first in the Sunday Express and latterly in the Mail on Sunday, were often rude and invariable partisan but he succintly put into writing what many ordinary readers thought.
Junor once described a former Archbishop of Canterbury as a "pathetic old man who deserves a kick up the backside," while former U.S. president George Bush was "a neutered old tabby."

A staunch right-winger, Junor was a firm believer in corporal punishment and despised leftists. The female anti-nuclear protesters who occupied a U.S. air base in Britain during the 1980s became the "Greenham Common sluts" and homosexuals were branded as "powder-puffs" and "pansies".
He backed Margaret Thatcher's radical right-wing policies, which transformed Britain and became known as Thatcherism, and he was knighted months after she came to power in 1979.
John Donald Brown Junor was born in a Glasgow tenement on January 15, 1919, the third son of a steelworks manager.
After studying at Glasgow University, he piloted bombers in World War Two. He then headed for politics, contesting unsuccessfully as a Liberal in various Scottish seats.
But publisher Lord Beaverbrook soon persuaded him to take up journalism, with the promise: "I will put a golden crown on your head."
Beaverbrook did not mislead Junor, who became assistant editor of the Daily Express from 1951 to 1953, deputy editor of the London Evening Standard in 1953 and editor of the Sunday Express in 1954.
It was a post he held for three decades, becoming the undisputed doyen of Fleet Street.
